notes:
Need to search first.I could only read three commentaries on Deuteronomy 14 before my search and fetch limit ran out, so most of what you asked for is missing.

**What these notes cover:**
- **Traditional reading (part 1):** David Guzik on enduringword.com (the English page and the Spanish version of the same commentary), Matthew Henry on blueletterbible.org, and preceptaustin.org. I only saw the parts of those pages that came back in one search, not the full pages. Most single verses inside vv. 4–20 have no notes.
- **Not covered:** Gill, Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary; part 2 (where Protestant traditions differ); and part 3 (modern scholarship, Catholic and Orthodox readings, prosperity teaching). I found nothing for these, so I've left them out.
- **Citations:** these are page URLs only. The search tool didn't give sentence references.

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik: the nations around Israel cut themselves or shaved the front of the head as part of funeral rites. Quoting Thompson, he says Israel was forbidden these practices because they meant copying pagans, and because the body was God's creation and shouldn't be disfigured. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-14/
- Guzik: Israel's hope in the living God stood against the hopelessness of pagan mourning. Christians shouldn't copy superstitious funeral customs or grieve like those without hope (1 Thess. 4:13). He quotes G. Campbell Morgan: even without clear certainty about life after death, Israel knew its attitude to death had to differ from people whose gods weren't real. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-14/ ; Morgan is named on the Spanish version: https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/deuteronomio-14/amp/
- Guzik (Spanish page, quoting Thompson): Israel didn't always keep this law, citing Jer. 41:5, Ezek. 7:18 and Amos 8:10. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/deuteronomio-14/amp/
- Matthew Henry: the Septuagint reads "be the children of the Lord" as a command, meaning act in a way fitting God's children. Some think the verse also forbids cutting oneself in idol worship, as Baal's prophets did. The body is for the Lord, so God's people shouldn't disfigure it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_014.cfm
- Henry also passes on a Jewish writer, quoted by Ainsworth, who reads the verse as a ban on excessive grief. If your father dies, you aren't fatherless, because the living God is your Father. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_014.cfm
- Precept Austin: Israel's status as God's sons rests on God choosing them to be a holy people, an adoption grounded in his love and undeserved favour. God also meant to use Israel to carry his promise to everyone. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-14-commentary

**v. 2**
- Guzik: "holy" means set apart. Believers in Jesus are also a holy nation (1 Pet. 2:9). Being holy, chosen and a treasured possession brings a matching responsibility to live differently among the nations. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-14/
- Henry: God set Israel apart for himself, so they shouldn't lower themselves by taking up idolaters' customs. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_014.cfm
- Precept Austin: holiness was Israel's position, and Moses calls for their daily practice to match it. Their way of life was to be a light showing the unseen God, and in the end the Messiah, to the nations. It links this to 1 Pet. 1:14–16. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-14-commentary

**vv. 3–21 (food laws in general)**
- Guzik sees three purposes:
  1. Health, by cutting out predators, scavengers and risky foods.
  2. A lesson about blood and the sacredness of life.
  3. Separation from the nations, since the laws made shared meals with Gentiles hard.

  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-14/
- Precept Austin: everything in Israel's daily life was to show its exclusive commitment to the Lord. Ritual uncleanness shut a person out of worship, and the lesson is that one must be clean to approach a holy God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-14-commentary

**vv. 6–8**
- Guzik: the test is simple. An animal had to have a split hoof (unlike the single hoof of a horse) and chew the cud. The camel, rock badger (hyrax) and hare chew the cud but have paws, not split hooves. The pig has a split hoof but doesn't chew the cud. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-14/

**vv. 9–10**
- Guzik: water creatures needed both fins and scales, so most fish were allowed, but catfish weren't. Clams, crabs, oysters and lobsters were unclean (Spanish page). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-14/ ; https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/deuteronomio-14/amp/

**vv. 11–20**
- Guzik: no general rule is given for birds, but the birds named as unclean are predators or scavengers. All winged insects are unclean. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-14/
- Precept Austin sets the NET and NLT wording of v. 19 side by side ("winged thing on the ground" and "winged insects that walk along the ground"). On v. 20 it just refers back to its note on v. 11. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-14-commentary

**v. 21**
- Carcasses: Guzik says an animal that died on its own hadn't been properly drained of blood. Blood stood for the life, which belongs to God alone (Lev. 17:11). https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/deuteronomio-14/amp/ ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-14/
- The young goat in its mother's milk:
  - Guzik takes it as a ban on copying a pagan fertility rite. He quotes Thompson, who says the same law appears in Exod. 23:19 and 34:26. It may reject a Canaanite custom described in a poem from Ugarit, an ancient Canaanite city.
  - Guzik also says observant Jews today keep meat and dairy apart (meals, plates, utensils), based on rabbinic reasoning.

  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-14/
- Precept Austin's preferred view ties the command back to v. 1, where Israelites weren't to carry signs of death on their bodies. It says the verse probably has nothing to do with the common Jewish practice of not eating meat with milk. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-14-commentary

**vv. 22–23**
- Guzik: "truly tithe" means a real ten percent, with no shortcuts. "Increase" probably means the grain left after seed was set aside, so the tithe was on income, not total assets. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-14/
- Guzik, quoting Thompson: harvest ceremonies were held at the Lord's sanctuary so that Canaanite gods wouldn't be honoured at harvest time. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-14/
- Guzik: the purpose of tithing was to build reverence for God, which he puts as teaching people to put God first. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-14/
- Henry: the harvest was tithed twice, so a fifth went to God in total. That was "an easy rent," because God's share was used for the people's own benefit. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_014.cfm

**vv. 24–26**
- Guzik: allowing the tithe to be turned into money shows how practical God's commands are. They weren't unreasonable, and they led Israel to rejoice. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-14/
- Henry: the tithe was brought to the sanctuary, as goods if convenient or else as its full value in money. It was then spent on a holy feast before the Lord. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_014.cfm
- I found nothing specifically on "wine, strong drink" in v. 26.

**v. 27**
- Guzik (Spanish page): God made his ministers depend on the people partly so they would be motivated to work for the people's spiritual good. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/deuteronomio-14/amp/

**vv. 28–29**
- Precept Austin: every third year a second tithe was stored in the hometown, not at the sanctuary. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-14-commentary
- Guzik takes a different view. Some see a separate "poor tithe," but because the text says "the tithe" and it also goes to the Levite, he thinks it was the same basic tithe, opened to the poor every third year. He sides with Kalland (another commentator) against the rabbinic idea of several tithes, and quotes Thompson calling it a local charity fund. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/deuteronomio-14/amp/
- Guzik on Christians today: tithing came before the Law (Heb. 7:5–9). Giving should be proportional, with ten percent a good starting point. For some even five percent is a big step of faith, and some early Christians said they weren't bound by the tithe because they could give more. The question shouldn't be "how little can I give?" https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/deuteronomio-14/amp/ ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-14/
- Henry: God cares for widows and orphans and wants us to as well. God's blessing is everything for material well-being, and it comes on those who work hard and give generously, not on the idle. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_014.cfm

**Searches still to run:** Gill, Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary on biblehub.com and studylight.org; Protestant views on whether the food laws and tithing apply to Christians today; the bibleodyssey.org and netbible.org notes on v. 21; Catholic and Orthodox views of the food laws; and prosperity teaching on tithing.
